title: Google Business Profile Categories: How to Choose the Right Ones
description: How to choose the primary and secondary categories on your Google Business Profile, with Valencia business examples, common mistakes and a quick checklist.

answer.question: How do I choose the category for my Google Business Profile?
answer.text: Choose as your primary category the one that best describes what your business IS to a customer (for example "Hair salon" or "Dental clinic"), not one specific product or service. Then add secondary categories only for other real activities you offer, starting with the most important. According to Google's official Business Profile help, you should pick the most specific category possible and you can add additional ones; avoid padding them with terms that do not describe you.

intro: The category is the smallest setting on your Google profile and also one of the most decisive: it tells Google who you are and which searches you can appear for. We explain how to choose the primary one, how many secondary ones to add and which mistakes to avoid, with examples of local businesses in Valencia.

body.question: How do I choose the category for my Google Business Profile?
body.text: Choose as your primary category the one that best describes what your business IS to a customer (for example "Hair salon" or "Dental clinic"), not one specific product or service. Then add secondary categories only for other real activities you offer, starting with the most important. According to Google's official Business Profile help, you should pick the most specific category possible and you can add additional ones; avoid padding them with terms that do not describe you.
Why the category is the most important setting on your profile

When someone searches "physiotherapist near me" or "garage in Valencia", Google has to decide which profiles match. The category is one of the clearest signals you give it: it tells Google which group of businesses you belong to. If you get it wrong, you may barely show up, or show up for people looking for something else, which means calls that are not meant for you.

The category also affects which features your profile shows: some options, such as bookings, menu or certain attributes, depend on the type of business. That is why it is worth spending ten calm minutes on it before touching anything else. This guide explains how to choose it, how to add secondary ones without overdoing it and how to change it without surprises.
Primary vs secondary: what each one does

The primary category is the one that best defines you. There is only one, and it is the one Google shows prominently on your profile, next to the reviews. Secondary categories describe other activities you genuinely carry out. Google lets you add several extra ones (up to nine in practice, according to what the profile editor itself shows), but being able to add them does not mean you should use them all.

A good rule of thumb: if a customer walking through your door asks about that service and you provide it without a problem, it can be a secondary category. If it is something you do once a year or that you would merely "like to offer", leave it out. Google does not publish how much each category weighs in rankings, so treat any exact figure you read elsewhere with caution.
How to choose your primary category, step by step

items: Think about how people search for you, not what you are called. A business named "Estilo Mediterráneo" is still a hair salon to the customer who types "hair salon near me".
Open the profile editor: search for your business on Google while signed in, click "Edit profile" and go to "Business information" to see the current category.
Type the first letters of your activity and review the suggestions. Google only lets you pick from its closed list, so you cannot invent categories.
Prefer the most specific option that is true. "Pizza restaurant" describes a pizzeria better than "Restaurant", and "Physiotherapist" is better than "Health centre".
Check which category the businesses ranking first for your search in your area use. Not to copy them blindly, but to see the vocabulary Google associates with your activity.
Save and wait. Changes can take a while to show and, in some cases, Google may review them.

body.text: Examples of local businesses in Valencia

items: Dog groomer in Ruzafa: the primary should be the one that defines the core service (pet grooming). If it also sells accessories and is genuinely a shop, "Pet store" can go in as a secondary; if it only sells four collars, it should not.

Rice restaurant in El Cabanyal: "Rice restaurant" as primary if it exists in the list, or the closest to what they are. A secondary such as "Mediterranean restaurant" is reasonable; "Bar" only if it genuinely works as a bar.
Physiotherapy clinic in Benimaclet: "Physiotherapist" as primary. If there is a distinct, stable service such as sports physiotherapy, you can consider a specific secondary.
Garage in Patraix: "Car repair shop" as primary; secondaries such as "Tyre shop" only if you have that service running every week.
English academy in Campanar: "Language school" or the most precise one available, not "Educational institution" or anything generic.

body.title: The three-question rule
body.text: Before adding a category, ask yourself: do I do this daily or nearly so? Could a customer ask for it today? Would I show it in my shop window? If the answer to all three is no, do not add it.
Common mistakes with categories

items: Choosing an aspirational category. Calling yourself "Luxury restaurant" or "Medical centre" without being one can lead to user complaints and problems with Google's guidelines on representing your business.
Filling all nine secondaries just in case. It dilutes your message and can show you for searches you cannot convert.

Stuffing keywords into the name instead of adjusting the category. Google's guidelines say the name must reflect the real name of the business; adding services or locations can trigger suspensions (we explain this in our guide on suspended profiles).
Changing the primary category every few weeks. If you see no improvement, the problem is usually elsewhere: reviews, photos, incomplete information or competition in the area.
Forgetting that the category depends on the premises. A business with no location open to the public needs to check whether it fits as a service-area business.

body.text: What happens if you change the primary category

You can change it whenever you like from the editor, but do it with a reason. Some businesses see temporary swings in searches after the change, and certain attributes or features may appear or disappear because they depend on the type of business. Note the date and compare performance in Google Search and Maps over the following weeks with the weeks before, which you can find in the performance section of your profile.

If your activity has genuinely changed, for example from a bar to a café with its own bakery, updating the category is correct and expected. If you just want to "test" whether it works better, it is best to change nothing until you have a clear hypothesis.
Category, services and description: make them say the same thing

The category does not work alone. On the same profile you can fill in the services or products section and the business description. Ideally all three tell the same story: if your primary is "Physiotherapist", your services should talk about physiotherapy, and your description about what kind of patients you see and in which neighbourhood. That consistency helps the user and stops the profile looking messy.

Do the same with your website. If your profile says "Dental clinic" and your home page talks about "wellbeing and holistic health", the customer senses an inconsistency and Google has fewer clear signals. One page per important service, using the same vocabulary as your profile, is usually a good next step. To go deeper, read our guide on what your customers search for and how to reflect it.
Checklist to review your categories today

body.title: 10-minute review
items: My primary category describes what I am, not one isolated service.
It is the most specific option that is still true.
Each secondary corresponds to a real service I provide regularly.
I have not added categories just to try to appear in more searches.
The profile name is the real one, with no added keywords.
Services and description are consistent with the categories.
My website says the same as my profile.
I have noted the date of any change so I can compare performance later.

body.text: When to ask for help

If your profile is suspended, duplicated or has a locked category, or if you are torn between several options because your business mixes activities, it is worth reviewing it with someone who has seen many cases. faq.q: How many categories can I have on my Google profile?
faq.a: One primary and several secondary. The profile editor lets you add up to nine additional ones, but you do not have to use them all; use only those that describe real services.

faq.q: Can I make up a category that is not in the list?
faq.a: No. Google only lets you choose from its predefined list of categories. If none fits exactly, pick the closest and complement it with services and description.

faq.q: Will changing the primary category make me lose rankings?
faq.a: There may be temporary swings, because the signal Google has about your business changes. If the new category describes you better, it usually pays off; note the date and compare performance.

faq.q: Does the category affect whether bookings, menu or other buttons appear?
faq.a: In some cases yes, because certain features and attributes depend on the type of business. Check in your editor which options appear after choosing the category.

faq.q: Should I put my neighbourhood or city in the category?
faq.a: No, categories are predefined. Location is determined by the address or service area on your profile.

faq.q: Which category do I choose if my business does several things?
faq.a: Choose as primary the activity that defines you most and brings the most customers, and leave the rest as genuine secondaries. If each activity is a separate business, consider whether they need separate profiles, always following Google's guidelines.
